prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Departures Board (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Flight" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 57px
  col 2: header "Destination" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 159px
  col 3: header "Scheduled" · longest unbreakable word 77px · one-line width 77px
  col 4: header "Estimated" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 73px
  col 5: header "Gate" · longest unbreakable word 34px · one-line width 34px
  col 6: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 68px · one-line width 107px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 558px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 557px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Help passengers find a flight and quickly check its destination, departure times, gate, and current status.","reading":"Readers locate a flight or destination, then scan across the row; scheduled and estimated times need to be easy to compare. Wrapping is most useful where another cell in the same row already makes the row taller.","groups":["Flight and Destination identify the departure.","Scheduled and Estimated are paired times and should have similar widths for comparison.","Gate and Status describe where to go and what is happening."],"keep_intact":["Individual flight numbers, times, gate codes, and single-word statuses.","The Scheduled and Estimated headers."],"may_wrap":["Multiword destinations at word boundaries, preferably without splitting flight identifiers in the same row.","Multiword statuses at word boundaries; a status can wrap within a row already made taller by its destination."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [78, 143, 98, 94, 55, 89] · table 558×278px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 36, 36, 36, 36] · column headers wrapped 0/6 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1B: widths [78, 137, 98, 94, 55, 95] · table 558×325px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 36, 36, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/6 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
